selected.name: Rich Conversational Subtext
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the dialogue implies a complex, ongoing relationship or an action just outside the frame, rather than merely commenting on the drawing. Score 0 if the caption is a direct, superficial observation of the cartoon with no implied backstory.
selected.rationale: Dense favors captions that expand the scene's narrative. R07 (getting rid of the lawyer) and R22 (john on the end) use rich subtext missed by the scorecard.

selected.name: Object-locked wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a pun depends precisely on an object, action, or setting shown in the cartoon; score 0 when it is a detachable homonym or word joke.
selected.rationale: R05 makes 'phase' depend on the moon, and R29 makes 'spare ribs' depend on both the tunnel's apparent anatomy and the chefs' menu.

selected.name: Topical Reference Self-Sufficiency
selected.instruction: Score how well the caption's humor stands on its own without relying on a topical, cultural, or celebrity reference as the primary comedic engine. A 10 means the caption is fully self-sufficient—any reference present is incidental to a joke that works on its own terms, or no reference is needed at all. A 0 means the caption's entire comedic value depends on recognizing a specific topical reference and removing it leaves nothing.
selected.rationale: The scorecard appears to reward topical references regardless of integration. Dense-low R41 ('easier to get than an N95 mask') and R53 ('his full 1200 stimulus') use the reference as the entire joke. Dense-high R25 embeds COVID references (masks, six feet) as secondary details inside a richer baseball scenario, and R40's ten-dollar-beer complaint is organic to the domestic situation.

selected.name: Cartoon-specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when replacing the cartoon with a different scene would break the caption’s meaning or humor; score 0 when the caption remains equally suitable for many unrelated cartoons.
selected.rationale: R02, R06, and R08 use broad real-estate concepts that transfer readily, while R16 and R58 depend on distinctive physical arrangements.

selected.name: Topical-reference integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural or current reference is tightly fused to the cartoon's visual premise; score 0 when the reference could be pasted onto almost any scene.
selected.rationale: R37 links baseball equipment and social distancing, while R48 makes the robot's grocery errand part of pandemic-era scarcity behavior.

selected.name: Implied aftermath
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the line suggests a vivid consequence, prior event, or next event beyond what is shown; score 0 when it stops at naming the visible oddity.
selected.rationale: R09 anticipates the need to catch the airborne guest, and R39 projects the future cost of removing the lawyer from the engine compartment.

selected.name: Relationship dynamics
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption establishes a specific power relationship, conflict, or intimacy between depicted participants; score 0 when it supplies no meaningful interpersonal dynamic.
selected.rationale: R17 and R28 exploit the boss-subordinate relationship created by the miniature self, while R55 builds a conflict between the wish-maker and the disappointed visitor.

selected.name: Punchline Economy And Anticlimax
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption uses very few words to abruptly cut the tension or create a comedic anticlimax. Score 0 if the caption is overly wordy or explains the joke too thoroughly.
selected.rationale: Short, punchy captions often score highly with dense models. R05 ('chicken or rabbit') and R44 ('arrive 20 minutes early') use brevity brilliantly to create an anticlimax.

selected.name: Obvious-Joke Subversion
selected.instruction: Score how well the caption avoids the single most obvious pun, wordplay, or joke available for the cartoon's premise and instead delivers a less expected angle. A 10 means the caption deliberately steers around the low-hanging fruit to find a fresher joke. A 0 means it delivers exactly the pun or joke that most people would think of first upon seeing the cartoon.
selected.rationale: The scorecard appears to reward any detectable wordplay regardless of originality. Dense-low entries like R24 ('new phase' for a moon), R58 ('downsizing' for a miniature boss), and R31 ('mid-life chrysalis' for butterfly wings) all deliver the most predictable pun and score high card, low dense. Meanwhile dense-high R27 extends the 'elephant in the room' idiom with a twist rather than merely stating it.

selected.name: Multi-detail integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the joke connects two or more conspicuous cartoon details in one coherent idea; score 0 when it uses only a generic reference to the overall oddity.
selected.rationale: R03 integrates the miniature person, human resources, and firing; R41 combines the elephant with the elevator idiom. R30 and R57 mainly attach a simple phrase to one visible feature.

selected.name: Coherent reframing
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption shifts the cartoon into an unexpected domain while preserving a clear structural mapping to the visible scene; score 0 when the new domain is merely associative or random.
selected.rationale: R04 reframes the faced moon through the poop-emoji comparison, and R59 maps the alien arrival onto a political firearm reference; R28 and R53 introduce topical associations with little structural mapping.

selected.name: Generic-prior obvious idiom
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption relies on the single most obvious idiom, pun, or literal interpretation directly invited by the visual elements of the scene. Do not judge whether the joke is clever or well-executed.
selected.rationale: General models often over-reward the consensus 'first-thought' reading of an image because it perfectly aligns text and image. R10 ('elephant in the room') and R23 ('downsizing') are the most predictable puns for their respective cartoons.
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream for the cartoon

selected.name: Topical news cycle reference
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption explicitly names or directly references a specific contemporary real-world entity, person, product, or event (e.g., 'n95 mask', 'stimulus', 'trump'). Do not judge if the reference is funny or apt, only how specific and time-bound the named entity is.
selected.rationale: Topical references are artifacts of the submission timing and may impress a scorecard looking for cleverness, but they are not inherent qualities of the caption for that specific cartoon (e.g., R24, R28).
upstream_parent_all_members: news cycle at the moment of the contest

selected.name: Practiced caption compression
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the line is compressed caption-native dialogue that assumes the drawing, omits explanation, and delivers one economical beat; do not judge whether the compression is effective.
selected.rationale: A serial entrant's familiarity with the format can leave disciplined brevity and refusal to narrate the image, while that same practice may also improve genuine writing skill. Compact examples include R03, R07, and R17.
upstream_parent_all_members: author's practice in the caption format
entrant’s serial practice in the format

selected.name: Transcription artifacts
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption exhibits catalog or transcription conventions such as lowercase starts, omitted terminal punctuation, ellipses, doubled hyphens, or spacing quirks; judge only visible text, not whether the caption is good.
selected.rationale: Lowercase presentation in R03, ellipses in R04, and doubled hyphens in R29 and R39 may come from compilation conventions rather than the entrant's wording or cartoon-specific quality.

selected.name: Generic caption polish
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption has compact, complete, immediately legible setup-punch packaging familiar from generic caption examples; do not judge whether it is funny or apt.
selected.rationale: Well-formed caption-shaped language is easy for a general-purpose prior to recognize without requiring contest-specific taste. R03, R20, R32, and R56 use concise, self-contained conventional joke formats.

selected.name: House-style tonal register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses plain, restrained, everyday conversational diction and understated social framing; do not judge whether that register suits the cartoon.
selected.rationale: A publication's recurring register can imprint captions with dry understatement and ordinary workplace or domestic diction, independently of cartoon-specific merit, while register can also affect contest suitability. Examples include R03, R17, and R42.

selected.name: Explicit scene explanation
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the caption names, paraphrases, or explains the visible anomaly or tells the reader how to interpret it; do not judge whether the explanation is effective.
selected.rationale: Explicit visual anchoring is a surface property that may be overvalued by generic text heuristics despite not being inherent quality. R35 spells out the “elephant in the room” premise, while R55 and R58 directly explain the bear or sheep-dog situation.

selected.name: Domestic-role framing
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption interprets the scene through family, spousal, household, neighbor, or parent-child roles and obligations; do not judge whether that framing is good.
selected.rationale: Entrant background and audience demographics can favor familiar domestic frames that correlate with reception but are not themselves evidence of cartoon fit. Examples include the wife in R05, father-and-son framing in R10, downstairs neighbors in R13, and marriage in R44.

selected.name: Bureaucratic or corporate jargon usage
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses specific corporate, bureaucratic, or administrative terminology (e.g., 'downsizing', 'litigation', 'human resources'). Do not judge if it fits the drawing well.
selected.rationale: Using corporate speak to contrast with an absurd visual is a very common contest template that mimics the magazine's historical style but is not inherently a better contest entry (e.g., R13, R02).

selected.name: Verbose conversational filler
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption uses spoken-style filler words (e.g., 'wow', 'sure', 'well', 'i guess') or conversational run-on phrasing to set up the punchline, adding words that do not change the core joke. Do not judge if the phrasing is good.
selected.rationale: Serial entrants often know that caption contest jokes require a specific spoken rhythm, but a dense model might discount excessive verbosity that doesn't add to the visual gag (e.g., R34, R42).
